title: Proper way to do window.opener()
body:
I just found something really neat from Google -

[https://developers.google.com/digital-asset-links/v1/getting-started](https://developers.google.com/digital-asset-links/v1/getting-started)

Instead of a current unsafe default for `window.opener()` - why doesn't the WhatWG specification make use of that Google innovation?

If a website is to allow other domains access via `window.opener()` it can declare that intent in a `assetlinks.json` file. If Site B isn't listed in Site A's `assetlinks.json` file and site B tries to use `window.opener()` then it returns null.

There were several documented MITM attacks involving Facebook and OAuth, this could help prevent that without breaking OAuth, `rel="noopener()"` won't.

That json file looks like it was designed for exactly this sort of thing - "The Digital Asset Links protocol and API enable an app or website to make public, verifiable statements about other apps or websites."

Applications that need to allow cross-domain access to `window.opener()` could declare such in the `assetlinks.json` file, a single place to manage those declarations and thus easy for security staff to monitor what websites a web application allows such modifications from.

It also avoids scenarios where a script injection results in a `window.open()` popunder that the `rel="noopener"` attribute can't possibly defend against. The attacker would not only need to pull off the script injection, but also modify the `assetlinks.json` file - which is easy to monitor and detect changes (and could have SELinux protections against modifications too at the discretion of competent system administrators)

There is some precedence too for json configuration of scripr behavior, Chrome requires a `manifest.json` file for their implementation of the PushAPI to work and that isn't a bad thing, it allows them to invalidate keys for abusers, a good thing for security.

Thoughts?
